full_judgment:
Fazle Hussain Mohammad Habibur Rahman, J.: Writ Petition No. 1731 of 1989 and Writ Petition No. 1737 of 1989 were heard together by a Division Bench consisting of MA Jalil and N Ahmed JJ. who could not agree with the decision of a Division Bench of this Court presided over by Mustafa Kamal, J in the case of Abdul Latif Vs. Bangladesh 43 DLR 446 with regard to the interpretation of the expression "person in the defence services of Bangladesh" as used in section 4 (3) of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980. So they referred the matter to the learned Chief Justice for constituting a Full Bench to dispose of the matter. The learned Chief Justice, however, constituted this Special Bench consisting of us to dispose of the matter. 

 6. Against both the officers proceedings were drawn up for committing misconduct under Rule 7 (2) of the Civilian Employees in Defence Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules 1961. They along with 52 others were also prosecuted under section 124A of the Penal Code in Gazipur Sessions Case No. 65 of 1990 arising out of GR Case No. 451 of 1987 arising out of Joydebpur PS Case No. 16(11) 87 and they were subsequently acquitted of the said charge by the Sessions Judge, Gazipur. 

 7. Petitioner SRK Lohani after the framing of the charge showed cause; the allegation against the petitioner was inquired into by an inquiring officer, namely, Lt. Col. Mujibur Rahman, Engineering Adviser of Ministry of Defence; evidence of the witnesses were taken and the petitioner cross-examined them. The inquiring officer found him guilty of misconduct and according to the Rule recommended punishment of compulsory retirement. Petitioner Lohani was also given a second show cause notice on 3.11.88 why he should not be compulsorily retired and after considering his reply dated 17.11.88 Mr. Md. Shamsul Huq Chisti, Secretary of the Ministry of Defence in exercise of his power under Rule 8(1)(f) of the Civilian Employees in Defence Services (Classification Control and Appeal) Rules, 1961 compulsorily retired the said petitioner by his order dated 9.7.89 (Annexure-H of his WP No. 1737 of 1989). 

 8. As already stated petitioner Serajul Islam Thakur was also prosecuted along with 53 other employees of the said Ordnance Factories under section 124A of the Penal Code in Gazipur Sessions Case No. 65 of 1990 arising out of GR Case No. 451 of 1987 arising out of Joydebpur PS Case No. 16 (11)87 in which case he was also acquitted on 28.4.92 by the Additional Sessions Judge, Gazipur. On 12.5.88 a charge of misconduct was drawn up against petitioner Serajul Islam Thakur under the said Rules and an explanation was called for from him as was done in the case of other petitioner. As the explanation given by petitioner Serajul Islam Thakur was not found satisfactory Lt. Col. Mujibur Rahman, Engineering Adviser, Ministry of Defence was appointed to inquire into the charges brought against the said petitioner. The inquiring officer examined 12 witnesses in the case of petitioner Lohani who cross-examined each of them and in the case of Serajul Islam Thakur 11 witnesses were examined and each of them was cross-examined by the petitioner Thakur. According to the provision of Rule 11(4) the inquiring officer submitted report finding them guilty of misconduct and recommended punishment of removal from service in the case of Thakur. On the basis of the report of the inquiring officer the Secretary, Ministry of Defence on 3.11.88 issued second show cause notice under Rule 9(4)(e) of the said Rule as to why he should not be removed from service. Petitioner Serajul Islam Thakur's reply dated 17.11.88 was not found to be satisfactory and Mr. Shamsul Huq Chisti, Secretary, Ministry of Defence in exercise of his power under Rule 8(1)(g) of the said Rules removed him from service by (Annexure-G) dated 9.7.89 of WP No. 1731 of 1989. 

 11. The charges framed against the two petitioners are Annexure-B dated 12.5.88 (against SRK Lohani of WP No. 1737/89) and Annexure-B dated 12.5.88 (against Serajul Islam Thakur of WP No. 1731/89). The inquiring officer in both the cases elaborately discussed the evidence against both the petitioner and submitted two different reports against them. The findings of the Inquiring Officer (Annexure-D) against petitioner Serajul Islam Thakur reads as follows: 

 12. We will presently show that the members of defence services as well as persons holding any civil post in the service of the Republic in view of the provision of Article 134 of the Constitution of Bangladesh hold office during the pleasure of the President but due to the protections given to the persons holding any civil post in the service of the Republic under Article 135 of the Constitution they are excluded from the mischief of the absolute doctrine of pleasure (vide AIR 1964 (SC) 600); but as the members of the service of defence have not been given any protection under the said Article 135 or any other Article of the Constitution, they can be retired, dismissed, removed and terminated at any time and against such orders passed against the members of the defence services they cannot come to the ordinary courts (that is Civil and Constitutional Courts) for any relief or redress against such orders. 

 13. However, assuming but not conceding that the petitioner can move this Court under Article 102(2)(i)(b) of the Constitution let us consider the arguments made by the learned Advocate for the petitioners in respect of the cases. 

 18. The learned Advocate for the petitioners next submits that Inquiring Officer showed his bad faith and bias by recommending in the inquiring report that the punishment against petitioner for the misconduct committed by him should be removal or retirement from service. There is no substance in this submission also as Rule 11(4) clearly provides that the inquiring officer shall submit has findings with grounds thereof and recommendation for penalty, if any, to the designated authority, who on receipt of the report shall take further action as laid down in Rule 9(4)(e). 

 20. The learned Advocate for the petitioner next submits that the appointment of Lt. Col. Mustafa Kamal as the conducting officer during the inquiry, who was also a Mamber of the preliminary inquiry committee constituted by the Chairman, Bangladesh Ordnance Factories Board has affected the impartiality of the inquiry made by Lt. Col. Mujibur Rahman and that, therefore, the impugned order of removal of the petitioners is bad in law on the ground of malafide. In the case of Jamil Hug Vs. Bangladesh 34 DLR (AD) 125 it has been held that malafide must be alleged and established by facts constituting malafide in a court of law. This principle is also judicially well-settled. It is easy on the part of any petitioner to make a vague allegation of malafide in each case; but it is well settled that malafide or bias is to be established by proved facts. Since the petitioners failed to allege malafide on proved facts in this case, therefore, there is no scope in law for this court in exercise of its summary jurisdiction under Article 102(2) of the Constitution to embark upon an inquiry on the allegation as alleged by the petitioner. 

 It can hardly be over-emphasised that the employees under the Ordinance Factories Board established under the Ordnance Factories Board Ordinance, 1961 (since repealed) are not civilian employees in any of the defence services but are pure and simple Government servants (i.e. persons holding civil posts in service of the Republic) serving under the said Board under the said Ordinance of 1961 and that the Ordnance Factories Board apparently under section 7 of the Ordnance Factories Board Ordinance, 1961 has merely for convenience adopted the Civilian Employees in Defence Services (Classification, Control, Appeal) Rules, 1961 which are similar to the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985 for regulating the terms, conditions, disciplinary matters, etc, of the employees of the Ordnance Factories Board. Merely because of the adaptation of the said Civilian Employees in Defence Services (Classification, Control, Appeal) Rules, 1961 by the Board for the disciplinary matters of the employees of the said Board, the said employees do not become members of the Defence services or Members of services in connection with the defence. The legal position is that before the said repealing Act No. 13 of 1989 came into force, the petitioners were Government servants (i.e. persons holding civil posts serving under the Ordnance Factories Board) and that after the repeal of the said Ordinance of 1961, because of Act No. 13 of 1989 they became Government servants (i.e. persons serving in civil posts in the service of the Republic) directly serving under the government within the meaning of Article 135 of the Constitution. A Division Bench of this Court presided over by Mustafa Kamal J in the case of Abdul Latif and another Vs. Government of Bangladesh. 43 DLR 446 has rightly taken the view that the Civilian Employees in the Defence Services (not being members of any of the defence services) are holders of Civil posts who now have to move the Administrative Tribunal (in view of Article 117 read with Article 102(5) of the Constitution) for redress of their grievances and cannot move the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. Therefore, the present petitioners before us do not come within the ambit of the expression person "in the Defence services of Bangladesh" as used in section 4(3) of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 (Act No. VII of 1981). 

 25. In the Constitution of India in Article 310(1) it is provided that every person who is a member of the defence service or of a civil service (of the Union or the State) or holds any post connected with defence services holds the same during the pleasure of the President or Governor of the State as the case may be an Article 311 of the Constitution of India gives protection to the persons holding civil posts under the Union or a State but neither Article 311 nor any other article of the Constitution of India gives any protection to the persons serving in the defence services or in any posts connected with defence. In the cases of LR Khurana Vs. Union of India, AIR 1971 (SC) 2111 and Union of India and another Vs. KS Subramanian, AIR 1976 (SC) 2433 it has been held that the persons serving in the defence services and holding post in connection with the defence are not protected by the conditions enumerated in Article 311 of the Constitution of India and as such are not entitled to any constitutional guarantee. 

 26. In the case of Bangladesh and others Vs. AKM Zahangir Hossain, 34 DLR (AD) 173 it has been observed by Kemaluddin Hossain, CJ as follows: 

 29. In the unreported cases of Rear Admiral A A Mustafa (WP No. 64/92) disposed of on 19th January, 1992 and Brigadier Abul Hasanat Md Abdullah (WP No. 154/87) two Division Benches of this Court have held that the members of Defence Service of the Republic hold office during the pleasure of the President which is not subject to any Constitutional guarantee and that they have no right in respect of their services to be enforced through a Court of Law and that they can be retired, removed or dismissed without assigning any reason whatsoever.
